Azure SQL Database to SQL Server (VM) with BACPAC, and Keeping It Encrypted with TDE

Nithin Sunke · November 2, 2026 · 18 min read

Lab 5 of the Azure SQL Database migration series, and the first move in the reverse direction. Azure SQL Database encrypts everything with TDE by default, but a BACPAC export silently drops that protection. This post exports a 16.8-million-row database out of Azure, imports it into SQL Server, and re-enables TDE two ways: with a certificate SQL Server generates itself, and with a certificate your organisation or customer provides.

Why BACPAC, and what happens to encryption

Azure SQL Database can't produce a native .bak backup, and it can't be a replication publisher. That leaves a BACPAC export as the standard way out. It's a logical export of schema and data, like Oracle expdp.

Azure SQL DB (TDE on) ──SqlPackage Export──▶ scsbank_azure.bacpac (NOT encrypted) ──SqlPackage Import──▶ SQL Server (TDE off)
                                                                                                     └─ enable TDE ─▶ encrypted again
StageEncrypted?
Azure database files and backupsYes: TDE, AES-256, on by default
Data in transit during exportYes: TLS
The .bacpac file on diskNo. Data is decrypted as it's read.
The imported database on SQL ServerNo. TDE doesn't travel with a BACPAC.

So this migration has two jobs: move the data, and restore the encryption at rest on the other side. The Oracle parallel is a Data Pump export without ENCRYPTION=ALL: the source tablespaces are encrypted, the dump file isn't.

Check TDE on the Azure source

At server level, SQL server → Security → Transparent data encryption shows who manages the key:

At database level, SQL database → Security → Data Encryption:

Or with T-SQL on cisql01/scsbank:

SELECT name, is_encrypted FROM sys.databases WHERE name = 'scsbank';      -- 1 = encrypted

SELECT DB_NAME(database_id) AS database_name, encryption_state_desc,
       key_algorithm, key_length, encryptor_type, percent_complete
FROM sys.dm_database_encryption_keys;

Protect the export folder

The BACPAC will hold the full dataset in plain form. Before writing it, restrict the folder to Administrators, SYSTEM and your own account:

mkdir B:\export
icacls "B:\export" /inheritance:r /grant:r "Administrators:(OI)(CI)F" "${env:USERNAME}:(OI)(CI)F" "SYSTEM:(OI)(CI)F"
Two gotchas here:
  • "$env:USERNAME:(OI)(CI)F" fails with Invalid parameter. PowerShell reads the colon as part of the variable name. Use ${env:USERNAME}.
  • Get-BitLockerVolume wasn't recognised: the BitLocker feature isn't installed, so the disk isn't BitLocker-encrypted. On OCI the block volume is still encrypted at rest by Oracle, but anyone who can log on to the VM can read the file. Folder permissions, and deleting the file promptly, are what protect it here.

Baseline and freeze the source

SELECT name, is_encrypted FROM sys.databases WHERE name = 'scsbank';

SELECT s.name, t.name, SUM(p.rows) AS row_count
FROM sys.tables t JOIN sys.schemas s ON t.schema_id = s.schema_id
JOIN sys.partitions p ON t.object_id = p.object_id AND p.index_id IN (0,1)
GROUP BY s.name, t.name ORDER BY 1,2;

SELECT type_desc, COUNT(*) FROM sys.objects WHERE is_ms_shipped = 0 GROUP BY type_desc ORDER BY 1;
SELECT SUM(Balance) AS total_balance FROM Account.Account;

Then stop writes. Check the editor header shows cisql01:

ALTER DATABASE scsbank SET READ_ONLY WITH ROLLBACK IMMEDIATE;

Export from Azure

Read the password without echoing it, then wake the serverless database first. The Lab 3 lesson: a paused database makes the first login time out.

$sec = Read-Host "Azure SQL password" -AsSecureString
$pwd = [Runtime.InteropServices.Marshal]::PtrToStringAuto(
         [Runtime.InteropServices.Marshal]::SecureStringToBSTR($sec))
sqlcmd -S tcp:cisql01.database.windows.net,1433 -d scsbank -U nsunke -P $pwd -l 120 -Q "SELECT 1" | Out-Null
sqlpackage /Action:Export `
  /SourceServerName:cisql01.database.windows.net /SourceDatabaseName:scsbank `
  /SourceUser:nsunke /SourcePassword:$pwd `
  /SourceEncryptConnection:True /SourceTimeout:120 `
  /TargetFile:"B:\export\scsbank_azure.bacpac" `
  /p:CommandTimeout=0

No TrustServerCertificate is needed: Azure's certificate is publicly trusted. Afterwards, reopen the source:

ALTER DATABASE scsbank SET READ_WRITE;     -- on cisql01

Import into SQL Server

A BACPAC from Azure can contain contained database users, whose passwords live inside the database. SQL Server rejects them unless contained authentication is enabled:

EXEC sp_configure 'contained database authentication', 1;
RECONFIGURE;

Contained authentication enabled

In this run I first created an empty scsbank database in SSMS, then imported into it:

Empty target database created in SSMS

sqlpackage /Action:Import `
  /SourceFile:"B:\export\scsbank_azure.bacpac" `
  /TargetServerName:MSSQLSRV01 /TargetDatabaseName:scsbank `
  /TargetTrustServerCertificate:True `
  /p:CommandTimeout=0
Pre-creating the database lets you choose file locations and sizes (data on D:\, log on L:\ here). If you let SqlPackage create it, the target name must not exist yet. /TargetTrustServerCertificate:True is only needed while the VM has a self-signed TLS certificate.

Check TDE on the target

Validate the data against the Azure baseline, and look at the encryption flag:

The data arrived intact, but unencrypted. Before enabling TDE, check what already exists in master so nothing is created twice:

USE master;
SELECT name FROM sys.symmetric_keys WHERE name = '##MS_DatabaseMasterKey##';     -- master key
SELECT name, subject, expiry_date FROM sys.certificates WHERE name LIKE 'TDE%';  -- TDE certificates

How the TDE key chain fits together

Service Master Key (SMK)          ← created at install, protected by Windows (DPAPI)
   └─ Database Master Key (DMK)   ← CREATE MASTER KEY in master
        └─ TDE certificate        ← generated (Option A) or imported (Option B)
             └─ Database Encryption Key (DEK, AES-256)   ← stored in the user database
                  └─ data and log pages on disk

The two options below differ only in where the certificate comes from. The database encryption key, SET ENCRYPTION ON and verification are identical.

Option A: SQL Server-generatedOption B: customer-provided
Who creates the key pairSQL Server (CREATE CERTIFICATE … WITH SUBJECT)Customer's PKI or key team
Who holds the master copyYou: back it up immediatelyThe customer, in their vault or HSM
Good forLabs, internal systems, DBA-owned keysRegulated environments, key custody and separation of duties

First, a folder for key files that the SQL Server service can write to. Run in an Administrator PowerShell:

mkdir B:\Keys
icacls "B:\Keys" /inheritance:r /grant:r "Administrators:(OI)(CI)F" "SYSTEM:(OI)(CI)F" "NT Service\MSSQLSERVER:(OI)(CI)M"

Certificate and key backups are written by the SQL Server service account, not your login. That's why NT Service\MSSQLSERVER needs Modify (M). (OI)(CI) applies it to files and subfolders.

Option A: TDE with a SQL Server-generated certificate

This is what I ran in the lab.

1Database master key in master, and back it up

USE master;
IF NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM sys.symmetric_keys WHERE name = '##MS_DatabaseMasterKey##')
    CREATE MASTER KEY ENCRYPTION BY PASSWORD = '<DMK_StrongPassword>';

BACKUP MASTER KEY TO FILE = 'B:\Keys\master_DMK.key'
    ENCRYPTION BY PASSWORD = '<DMK_Backup_Password>';

2Generate the TDE certificate

USE master;
CREATE CERTIFICATE TDE_Cert
    WITH SUBJECT = 'TDE certificate for scsbank_from_azure',
         EXPIRY_DATE = '2036-12-31';
  • SQL Server creates an RSA key pair and stores it in master, with the private key encrypted by the master key. No file is written yet.
  • SUBJECT is only a label.
  • Without EXPIRY_DATE, the default is one year. TDE ignores expiry, so a far-future date just avoids warnings.
  • It isn't a TLS certificate and doesn't encrypt anything on its own.

3Back up the certificate immediately

BACKUP CERTIFICATE TDE_Cert
    TO FILE = 'B:\Keys\TDE_Cert.cer'
    WITH PRIVATE KEY (FILE = 'B:\Keys\TDE_Cert.pvk',
                      ENCRYPTION BY PASSWORD = '<Cert_Backup_Password>');
Copy TDE_Cert.cer, TDE_Cert.pvk, master_DMK.key and their passwords off the server. Without them, this database's backups can never be restored anywhere else. Losing them is like losing an Oracle TDE wallet.

4Create the database encryption key

USE scsbank;
CREATE DATABASE ENCRYPTION KEY
    WITH ALGORITHM = AES_256
    ENCRYPTION BY SERVER CERTIFICATE TDE_Cert;

5Turn encryption on

USE master;
ALTER DATABASE scsbank SET ENCRYPTION ON;

Database encryption key created, encryption switched on

Encryption runs online in the background. Every page is read, encrypted and written back while the database stays available.

Option B: TDE with an imported customer certificate

When the organisation or customer supplies the certificate, you import it instead of generating one. Everything from the database encryption key onwards is the same as Option A.

What to ask for

ItemRequirement
Certificate with private keyA .pfx (PKCS#12), or a .cer + .pvk pair. A .cer alone (public key only) can't be used for TDE.
PasswordSent through a different channel from the file
Key typeRSA, 2048 bits or more
ThumbprintTo confirm you imported the right certificate
Custody agreementWho keeps the master copy, who does DR restores, and the rotation schedule

TDE ignores the certificate's expiry and Key Usage, so it doesn't need the Server Authentication usage that TLS certificates need.

1Stage the file where SQL Server can read it

mkdir B:\Keys\import
icacls "B:\Keys\import" /inheritance:r /grant:r "Administrators:(OI)(CI)F" "SYSTEM:(OI)(CI)F" "NT Service\MSSQLSERVER:(OI)(CI)R"
# copy the customer file here, e.g. B:\Keys\import\Customer_TDE.pfx

2Database master key in master

USE master;
IF NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM sys.symmetric_keys WHERE name = '##MS_DatabaseMasterKey##')
    CREATE MASTER KEY ENCRYPTION BY PASSWORD = '<DMK_StrongPassword>';

3Import the customer certificate

From a .pfx (SQL Server 2022 and later):

CREATE CERTIFICATE Customer_TDE_Cert
    FROM FILE = 'B:\Keys\import\Customer_TDE.pfx'
    WITH FORMAT = 'PFX',
    PRIVATE KEY (DECRYPTION BY PASSWORD = '<pfx_password_from_customer>');

From a .cer + .pvk pair (any version):

CREATE CERTIFICATE Customer_TDE_Cert
    FROM FILE = 'B:\Keys\import\Customer_TDE.cer'
    WITH PRIVATE KEY (FILE = 'B:\Keys\import\Customer_TDE.pvk',
                      DECRYPTION BY PASSWORD = '<pvk_password>');

4Confirm it's the right certificate, with its private key

SELECT name, subject, issuer_name, expiry_date,
       pvt_key_encryption_type_desc,   -- must be ENCRYPTED_BY_MASTER_KEY
       key_length, thumbprint
FROM master.sys.certificates WHERE name = 'Customer_TDE_Cert';
  • Compare thumbprint with the value the customer gave you.
  • NO_PRIVATE_KEY means you only received the public part. Go back to the customer.

5Database encryption key and encryption on

USE scsbank;
CREATE DATABASE ENCRYPTION KEY
    WITH ALGORITHM = AES_256
    ENCRYPTION BY SERVER CERTIFICATE Customer_TDE_Cert;

USE master;
ALTER DATABASE scsbank SET ENCRYPTION ON;

6Remove the staged copy

Remove-Item B:\Keys\import\* -Force

The customer keeps the master copy, so don't leave a second one on the server. Record the certificate name and thumbprint in your runbook.

Older SQL Server (2019 and earlier) can't read .pfx directly. Convert it to .cer + .pvk with OpenSSL first, then delete the intermediate .pem files, because they contain the unencrypted private key.
Customer won't release the private key? Use Extensible Key Management (EKM), for example the SQL Server Connector for Azure Key Vault. The database encryption key is then protected by an asymmetric key that stays in the customer's vault or HSM, and they can revoke access at any time. That's the on-premises equivalent of Azure SQL's customer-managed key TDE.

Verify encryption and backups

These checks apply to both options:

SELECT DB_NAME(database_id) AS database_name, encryption_state_desc,
       percent_complete, key_algorithm, key_length, encryptor_type
FROM sys.dm_database_encryption_keys;
Why tempdb? As soon as any database on an instance uses TDE, SQL Server encrypts tempdb as well, so temporary data from the encrypted database can't leak to disk unencrypted.
SELECT name, is_encrypted FROM sys.databases WHERE name IN ('scsbank','tempdb');   -- both 1

Finally, prove the whole chain works with an encrypted backup:

BACKUP DATABASE scsbank TO DISK = 'B:\Backup\scsbank_tde.bak'
    WITH COMPRESSION, CHECKSUM, INIT;
RESTORE VERIFYONLY FROM DISK = 'B:\Backup\scsbank_tde.bak' WITH CHECKSUM;

Source and target side by side

Azure (source)SQL Server VM (target)
is_encrypted11
StateENCRYPTEDENCRYPTED
AlgorithmAES-256AES-256
Key protectorService-managed (Azure)TDE_Cert in master (Option A), or the customer certificate (Option B)
Key backupAzure's responsibilityYours (A) or the customer's (B)
Rows / objects / balanceIdentical: 16,760,354 rows, 17 tables, 749,873,497,000.00

Then delete the BACPAC. It's the one unencrypted copy of the data:

Remove-Item "B:\export\scsbank_azure.bacpac" -Force

Restoring on another server

Any server that restores these backups must have the same certificate first:

USE master;
IF NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM sys.symmetric_keys WHERE name = '##MS_DatabaseMasterKey##')
    CREATE MASTER KEY ENCRYPTION BY PASSWORD = '<NewServer_DMK_Password>';

-- Option A: from your backup files
CREATE CERTIFICATE TDE_Cert
    FROM FILE = 'B:\Keys\TDE_Cert.cer'
    WITH PRIVATE KEY (FILE = 'B:\Keys\TDE_Cert.pvk',
                      DECRYPTION BY PASSWORD = '<Cert_Backup_Password>');

-- Option B: from the customer's .pfx (same CREATE CERTIFICATE ... FORMAT = 'PFX' as above)

RESTORE DATABASE scsbank FROM DISK = 'B:\Backup\scsbank_tde.bak'
    WITH MOVE 'scsbank' TO 'D:\Data\scsbank.mdf', MOVE 'scsbank_log' TO 'L:\Log\scsbank_log.ldf';

Without the certificate, the restore fails with "Cannot find server certificate with thumbprint 0x…". That error is TDE doing its job.

Rotating the certificate later

USE master;
CREATE CERTIFICATE TDE_Cert_2027 WITH SUBJECT = 'TDE certificate 2027';   -- or import the customer's new one
BACKUP CERTIFICATE TDE_Cert_2027 TO FILE = 'B:\Keys\TDE_Cert_2027.cer'
    WITH PRIVATE KEY (FILE = 'B:\Keys\TDE_Cert_2027.pvk', ENCRYPTION BY PASSWORD = '<pwd>');

USE scsbank;
ALTER DATABASE ENCRYPTION KEY ENCRYPTION BY SERVER CERTIFICATE TDE_Cert_2027;

Rotation only re-protects the database encryption key: it's instant, with no data re-encryption. Keep the old certificate until every backup made under it has expired.

Troubleshooting

ProblemCauseFix
Get-BitLockerVolume not recognisedBitLocker feature not installedRely on volume encryption and folder ACLs, or install BitLocker (needs a reboot)
icacls: Invalid parameter "(OI)(CI)F"$env:USERNAME: read as one variableUse ${env:USERNAME}
Export: login timeoutServerless database pausedWarm-up query and /SourceTimeout:120
Import: containment errorContained users from Azuresp_configure 'contained database authentication', 1
Import: "object [scsbank] exists in the target" warningsPre-created database filesExpected. No action needed.
"Please create a master key in the database"CREATE CERTIFICATE run before CREATE MASTER KEYCreate the master key first
BACKUP CERTIFICATE: Access is deniedSQL Server service can't write to B:\KeysGrant NT Service\MSSQLSERVER Modify
Warning: certificate has not been backed upCertificate backup skippedRun BACKUP CERTIFICATE. Don't ignore it.
Imported certificate shows NO_PRIVATE_KEYCustomer sent only the public .cerAsk for a .pfx or a .cer + .pvk pair
Encryption stuck in progressLarge database, or the database is read-onlyWatch percent_complete; set READ_WRITE first
Restore elsewhere: "Cannot find server certificate with thumbprint"Certificate missing on that serverRestore or import the certificate first

Results and takeaways

MetricValue
Export from Azure1 min 16 s
Import into SQL Server5 min 47 s
Data validation17/17 tables, 16,760,354 rows, objects and balance total identical
TDE on targetENCRYPTED, AES-256, tempdb included
Encrypted backup333,994 pages in 67 s, verified
  • BACPAC is the way out of Azure SQL Database, and it's fast for a few GB.
  • Encryption doesn't come with you. The BACPAC file and the imported database are both unencrypted until you act. Protect the file and delete it promptly.
  • Re-enabling TDE takes five statements: master key, certificate, certificate backup, database encryption key, SET ENCRYPTION ON.
  • Choose the certificate source by who should own the key. Generate it when the DBA team owns the keys. Import it when the customer or security team must keep custody. Use EKM when the key must never leave their vault.
  • In Azure, key management was invisible. On SQL Server, the certificate backup is your responsibility. Without it, your encrypted backups are unrecoverable.
